name: Ask for the denominator
short: Out of how many? Turn counts and percentages back into natural frequencies.
text: Ask how common the thing is to begin with, and what the numbers are out of. Base rates, absolute risks and the reverse probability fall out of one 2×2 table.

name: Compared with what?
short: Ask for the group that didn't get it, over the same time.
text: A change or a link means little without a fair comparison: a control group, the same people before, or similar places that were left alone.

name: Draw the causal diagram
short: Sketch what causes what, then look for back doors and colliders.
text: Draw arrows between exposure, outcome and everything that affects them. Paths through a common cause need adjusting for; a common effect must not be selected on.

name: Check the timeline
short: What came first, and when did each person's clock start?
text: Line up when exposure, diagnosis, follow-up and outcome happened. Causes come first; follow-up starts at the same moment for every group.

name: Plot it over time
short: Look at the whole series, not two points or one stretch.
text: A longer series shows trends, bounces back to normal and breaks where a definition changed. Compare year-on-year changes, not levels.

name: Split by subgroup
short: Break the total down by the variable that differs between groups.
text: Look within departments, hospitals, age bands or severity levels. If the comparison flips, decide which level answers the question.

name: Ask for individual data
short: Do the same people have both traits, or only the same places?
text: A claim about people needs data on people. Group averages can't show who within the group has the exposure and the outcome.

name: Find who's missing
short: Who dropped out, failed, didn't answer or never got in?
text: List how cases reached the data set. Survivors, responders, admitted patients and published studies are filtered, and the filter can create the result.

name: Check who and what was studied
short: Which people, species, doses and years does the evidence cover?
text: Compare the claim's reach with the data's range. Outside the studied population, dose or period, the result is a hypothesis.

name: Find the preregistration
short: Was this outcome and analysis planned before the data came in?
text: Look for a trial registration or preregistered plan and compare it with the paper. Switched outcomes and unplanned subgroups are exploratory.

name: Look for the other studies
short: Has it been replicated? What do registries and reviews show?
text: Search for replications, systematic reviews and registered trials, including unpublished ones. One result is a lead; a body of evidence is a finding.

name: Read the confidence interval
short: Look at the range of effects the data allow, not just the p-value.
text: A wide interval means the data are compatible with large effects in both directions, or none. Small samples give wide intervals.

name: Ask how big
short: How large is the effect in units that matter to people?
text: Ask for the absolute difference, the number needed to treat, or the effect in real units, and compare it with what would matter in practice.

name: Ask what was measured
short: Is the outcome the thing we care about, measured the same way throughout?
text: Check whether the result is a marker or the real endpoint, and whether definitions, tests or screening changed during the study.

name: Test it on new data
short: How well does it predict cases it has never seen?
text: Ask for performance on held-out or later data, or an external validation. Fit on the data used to build a model is always flattering.

name: Read the axes
short: Where does each axis start, and are the scales the same?
text: Check the axis start, units, scale and time window. Redraw from zero, or on one scale, and see if the story survives.
